questions.prompt: A severely injured patient is cold, acidotic, and bleeding with impaired clot formation. Which combination is the trauma lethal triad?

options.A: Trauma-related coagulopathy can manifest as abnormal clot formation or fibrinolysis.
options.B: Hypothermia and acidosis can prevent thrombin generation.
options.C: Hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy.
options.D: Use early hemorrhage control, permissive hypotension until control, avoid crystalloids, and give early blood components.

questions.rationale: The patient’s cold, acidotic, bleeding state points to the classic trauma lethal triad. Stoelting identifies the three components as hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy, making C the complete answer.

optionExplanations.A: Trauma-related coagulopathy can involve abnormal clot formation or fibrinolysis, but this is only one component and does not name the lethal triad.
optionExplanations.B: Hypothermia and acidosis can impair thrombin generation, but the pair omits coagulopathy and therefore is not the complete triad.
optionExplanations.C: C directly gives all three stored components of the trauma lethal triad: hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy.
optionExplanations.D: Early hemorrhage control and damage-control resuscitation are related management measures, but this option describes treatment rather than the triad’s components.

sources: Stoelting P&P 6e (2022).pdf — 31. Physiology and Management of Massive Transfusion — PDF p. 2054
Stoelting Coexisting 8e (2021).pdf — 4 Critical illness — PDF p. 73
questions.evidenceSufficiency: The stored Stoelting passages directly support C and distinguish component-level mechanisms from resuscitation measures.

questions.prompt: In a trauma patient undergoing focused assessment with sonography, what is the primary goal of the FAST examination?

options.C: Perform subxiphoid, right-flank, left-flank, and suprapubic views.
options.D: Detect pathologic free fluid in the pericardial, peritoneal, and pleural cavities.

optionExplanations.A: CT may be used when FAST is negative but suspicion remains high, but that is a follow-up strategy and not FAST’s primary goal.
optionExplanations.B: An anterior thoracic view is an extended-FAST addition for pneumothorax, but it does not define the primary FAST target asked for.
optionExplanations.C: The subxiphoid, flank, and suprapubic views describe standard FAST acquisition, but they are the examination’s views rather than its diagnostic goal.
optionExplanations.D: D directly states the stored Barash purpose of FAST: detect pathologic free fluid in the pericardial, peritoneal, and pleural cavities.

questions.prompt: A patient with severe intracranial hypertension develops hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respirations. Which finding is present?

options.A: Cushing triad due to brainstem dysfunction.
options.B: The Cushing reflex raises systemic blood pressure above intracranial pressure.
options.C: Irregular respirations are often absent because severe cases are mechanically ventilated.
options.D: The central nervous system ischemic reflex can produce profound systemic hypertension.

questions.rationale: The combination of hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respirations in severe intracranial hypertension is the Cushing triad. Stoelting attributes the triad to brainstem dysfunction, so A is the direct finding.

optionExplanations.A: A directly identifies the stored finding: Cushing triad consists of hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respirations from brainstem dysfunction.
optionExplanations.B: The Cushing reflex can raise systemic blood pressure above intracranial pressure, but that mechanism alone does not identify the triad finding asked for.
optionExplanations.C: Mechanical ventilation can obscure irregular respirations in some severe cases, but the stem asks which triad is present and includes the classic respiratory component.
optionExplanations.D: The central nervous system ischemic reflex can produce profound hypertension, but it is a different reflex and does not name the triad in the stem.

sources: Stoelting P&P 6e (2022).pdf — 14. Circulatory Physiology — PDF p. 1196

questions.prompt: A neurocritical-care monitor shows MAP and intracranial pressure. Which relationship calculates cerebral perfusion pressure?

options.A: CPP is preserved when ICP decreases more than MAP after barbiturate administration.
options.B: Cerebral perfusion pressure equals mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure.
options.C: Sufentanil-related ICP increases occurred only with a decrease in MAP.
options.D: Barbiturates reduce cerebral metabolic rate with parallel reductions in cerebral blood flow and ICP.

questions.rationale: The monitor provides MAP and intracranial pressure, and cerebral perfusion pressure is the difference between those pressures. Miller states CPP equals MAP minus ICP, directly supporting B.

optionExplanations.A: The frozen A option describes conditional CPP preservation after barbiturate administration when ICP falls more than MAP; it is not the barbiturate metabolic-rate and CBF reduction statement.
optionExplanations.B: B directly states the stored relationship: cerebral perfusion pressure equals mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure.
optionExplanations.C: The sufentanil observation concerns when ICP increased, but it does not provide the general CPP relationship between MAP and ICP.
optionExplanations.D: The frozen D option describes barbiturate reductions in cerebral metabolic rate, CBF, and ICP, but it is not the conditional CPP-preservation statement in A.

sources: Miller 10e (2024).pdf — 21. Intravenous Anesthetics — PDF p. 631

questions.prompt: A critically ill patient may require extracorporeal support for predominant respiratory failure, cardiogenic shock, or combined organ failure. Which statement should guide selection of the ECMO configuration?

options.B: ECMO should be viewed as bridging therapy toward recovery or replacement of a failing heart, lung, or both.
options.C: ECMO configurations such as VV and VA are selected according to whether respiratory failure, cardiogenic shock, or combined organ failure predominates.
options.D: Peripheral VA cannulation is the most rapid way to initiate urgent ECMO outside cardiac surgery.

questions.rationale: The required ECMO configuration depends on the dominant failing organ system. Miller states that VV and VA configurations are selected according to respiratory failure, cardiogenic shock, or combined organ failure, so C is the decisive answer.

optionExplanations.C: C directly applies Miller’s configuration rule: select VV or VA according to whether respiratory failure, cardiogenic shock, or combined organ failure predominates.
optionExplanations.D: Peripheral VA cannulation may be rapid in urgent settings, but that procedural point does not establish configuration selection by the dominant organ failure.

questions.prompt: According to Barash 9th edition, which statement combines permanence of cerebral and brainstem function loss with correction of reversible causes in brain-death determination?

options.B: Ancillary tests such as cerebral angiography, transcranial Doppler, or EEG can confirm the examination when clinical criteria are incomplete.

optionExplanations.B: Ancillary testing can help when clinical criteria are incomplete, but the option does not state the required permanent loss and correction of reversible causes.
optionExplanations.C: Unresponsiveness and absent brainstem reflexes are findings in a brain-death examination, but this option omits permanence and correction of reversible causes.
optionExplanations.D: D combines both decisive requirements from Barash: permanent absence of cerebral and brainstem function after reversible causes of coma have been corrected.

questions.prompt: Which principle explains how pulse oximetry estimates arterial hemoglobin oxygen saturation?

options.A: Blood oxygen content combines dissolved oxygen with oxygen bound as haemoglobin.
options.B: At approximately 660 nm, oxyhaemoglobin and deoxyhaemoglobin differ widely in absorbance.
options.C: Pulse oximetry estimates hemoglobin saturation by comparing absorption at two wavelengths and correcting for arterial pulsation.
options.D: Oxyhaemoglobin and deoxyhaemoglobin have similar absorbance at approximately 940 nm.

questions.rationale: Pulse oximetry estimates saturation by using the differing wavelength absorption of oxyhaemoglobin and deoxyhaemoglobin while isolating the pulsatile arterial component. Stoelting describes that comparison and correction, supporting C.

optionExplanations.A: Blood oxygen content includes dissolved and haemoglobin-bound oxygen, but content is not the optical saturation-estimation principle asked for.
optionExplanations.B: The large absorbance difference near 660 nm is part of the optical basis, but it does not by itself describe comparing two wavelengths and correcting for pulsation.
optionExplanations.C: C directly states the stored principle: compare absorption at two wavelengths and use arterial pulsation to estimate haemoglobin saturation.
optionExplanations.D: Similar absorbance near 940 nm contributes to the optical method, but this partial fact does not state the full pulse-oximetry calculation principle.

sources: Stoelting P&P 6e (2022).pdf — 24. Gas Exchange — PDF p. 1775

questions.prompt: During pulmonary-artery-catheter monitoring, cold saline is injected and the change in blood temperature is measured. What principle determines the thermodilution cardiac output?

optionExplanations.B: Indocyanine-green dilution and area-under-the-curve analysis are an indicator-dye method, but they are not the cold-saline thermodilution principle described.
optionExplanations.C: Early indicator-dye recirculation may suggest a right-to-left shunt, but this interpretation is not the cardiac-output principle in the stem.
optionExplanations.D: The catheter ports and distal temperature sensor are required hardware, but they do not state how the temperature change determines output.

sources: Stoelting P&P 6e (2022).pdf — 14. Circulatory Physiology — PDF p. 1209

sources: Miller 10e (2024).pdf — 32. Cardiovascular Monitoring — PDF p. 1205

questions.prompt: A capnogram has an upward-sloping alveolar plateau, while another has a slow second-phase upstroke. Which interpretation correctly matches these patterns?

optionExplanations.A: A directly matches Barash’s waveform interpretation: the upward plateau slope indicates ventilation-perfusion mismatch and the slow second-phase upstroke suggests obstruction.
optionExplanations.B: The first phase samples anatomic dead space and is normally carbon-dioxide free, but that normal phase does not explain the two abnormal patterns in the stem.
optionExplanations.C: An inspiratory baseline near zero is expected without rebreathing, but it does not interpret the upward plateau and slow upstroke described.
optionExplanations.D: End-tidal carbon dioxide is the highest value and reflects alveolar gas, but that definition does not match the paired capnogram-pattern question.

sources: Barash 9e (2023).pdf — 26. Commonly Used Monitoring Techniques — PDF p. 2108

questions.prompt: Why must a circle breathing system remove carbon dioxide from exhaled gas?

questions.prompt: Which contemporary vaporizer safety feature prevents simultaneous administration of more than one inhaled volatile anaesthetic?

options.A: Securing the vaporizer to the workstation manifold with antispill protection.
options.B: An interlock system.
options.C: A filler port located at the maximum safe liquid level.
options.D: Agent-specific keyed filling devices.

questions.rationale: The safety feature must prevent two volatile agents from being delivered simultaneously. Barash identifies the vaporizer interlock system as performing that function, directly supporting B.

optionExplanations.C: A maximum-level filler port helps control filling, but it is not the interlock mechanism that prevents simultaneous vaporizer use.

options.A: Pheochromocytoma preparation includes alpha-adrenergic receptor blockade and intravascular volume repletion.
options.B: Most patients require 7 to 14 days of treatment to meet criteria for adequate preoperative alpha-adrenergic blockade.
options.C: Beta-adrenergic blockade must be preceded by effective alpha-adrenergic blockade to prevent a paradoxical hypertensive response.
options.D: Pheochromocytoma carries risk of severe hypertension during induction and tumor manipulation and severe hypotension after tumor excision.

questions.rationale: Pheochromocytoma preparation combines alpha blockade with intravascular volume repletion, particularly when depletion persists. Chestnut supports A.

optionExplanations.A: A directly states Chestnut’s required preparation: alpha-adrenergic blockade and intravascular volume repletion.
optionExplanations.B: Seven to fourteen days may be needed for adequate alpha blockade, but duration alone does not include correction of volume depletion.
optionExplanations.C: Alpha blockade must precede beta blockade to prevent paradoxical hypertension, but that sequence does not state volume repletion.
optionExplanations.D: Severe hypertension during manipulation and hypotension after excision are important risks, but they are not the preparation elements asked for.

questions.prompt: Why can a large substernal goiter cause dangerous airway obstruction after induction?

options.A: Long-standing goiters require extubation under optimal circumstances for reintubation if tracheomalacia is present.
options.B: Large substernal goiters can behave as anterior mediastinal masses and cause intrathoracic airway obstruction after induction of general anesthesia.
options.C: Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causes stridor and laryngeal obstruction from unopposed vocal-cord adduction.
options.D: Neuromuscular blocking drugs must be avoided after intubation when recurrent-laryngeal-nerve neuromonitoring is used.

questions.rationale: A large substernal goiter can behave like an anterior mediastinal mass, causing intrathoracic airway obstruction after induction. Barash supports B.

optionExplanations.A: Optimal extubation planning is important when tracheomalacia is present, but it does not explain postinduction obstruction from a substernal mass.
optionExplanations.B: B directly states Barash’s mechanism: a large substernal goiter can act as an anterior mediastinal mass and obstruct the intrathoracic airway after induction.
optionExplanations.C: Recurrent-laryngeal-nerve injury can cause stridor and obstruction, but that neural injury is a different mechanism from the substernal mass effect.
optionExplanations.D: Neuromuscular blockers may be avoided during nerve monitoring, but that intraoperative constraint does not explain postinduction mass-related airway obstruction.

questions.prompt: Which anesthetic conditions facilitate perfusion of a free flap during reconstructive surgery?

options.A: Free flaps involve reanastomosis of vessels from a distant donor site to recipient-site vessels.
options.B: Pressors such as phenylephrine or norepinephrine are discouraged because they may compromise graft perfusion.
options.C: Free-flap anesthetic care should facilitate graft-vessel perfusion by keeping the patient warm, euvolemic, and comfortable.
options.D: Elective free-flap procedures tend to be long-duration operations conducted using general anesthesia.

questions.rationale: Free-flap perfusion is supported by maintaining warmth, euvolemia, and comfort, thereby facilitating graft-vessel flow. Miller supports C.

optionExplanations.A: Free flaps do involve reanastomosis of distant donor vessels, but that definition does not state the anesthetic conditions supporting perfusion.
optionExplanations.B: Pressors may be used cautiously because perfusion concerns exist, but this statement does not give the complete warmth, volume, and comfort strategy.
optionExplanations.C: C directly states Miller’s free-flap anesthetic goals: keep the patient warm, euvolemic, and comfortable to facilitate graft-vessel perfusion.
optionExplanations.D: Free-flap procedures are often long and use general anesthesia, but duration and anesthetic type do not state perfusion-support conditions.

questions.prompt: Why does the same inspired gas fraction produce a reduced anesthetic effect at high altitude?
questions.domain: Domain 14 · Remote extreme-environment and disaster anesthesia

options.A: Lack of adaptation at high altitude can lead to acute mountain sickness, high-altitude pulmonary edema, decompression illness, or acute worsening of comorbid conditions.
options.B: These high-altitude illnesses can rapidly become fatal if not treated appropriately, including with descent to lower altitudes.
options.C: Providing critical care or anesthesia in extreme environments is complicated by their extreme remoteness and requires robust, simple health-care protocols.
options.D: At high altitude, relative concentrations of gases including oxygen remain static, but falling atmospheric pressure decreases the partial pressure of each gas.

questions.rationale: At high altitude the gas fractions remain relatively unchanged, but lower atmospheric pressure lowers each gas’s partial pressure and reduces anesthetic effect. Miller supports D.

optionExplanations.A: High-altitude illness includes mountain sickness, pulmonary edema, decompression illness, and worsening comorbidity, but those disorders do not explain reduced anesthetic partial pressure.
optionExplanations.B: High-altitude illnesses can be fatal and may require descent, but that clinical danger does not state why the same fraction has less effect.
optionExplanations.C: Remoteness complicates critical care and requires robust protocols, but logistics do not explain the partial-pressure change.
optionExplanations.D: D directly states Miller’s physical explanation: atmospheric pressure falls while relative gas concentrations remain static, lowering every gas’s partial pressure.

sources: Miller 10e (2024).pdf — 70. Clinical Care in Extreme Environments: Physiology at High Altitude and in Space — PDF p. 2641
questions.evidenceSufficiency: The stored Miller passage directly supports D and distinguishes illness, logistics, and gas-law explanations.

questions.prompt: During a disaster with a fluid shortage, how should limited medications, fluids, and kits be allocated?
questions.domain: Domain 14 · Remote extreme-environment and disaster anesthesia

options.A: During a fluid shortage in a disaster, resources should be used only with confirmation of patient need.
options.B: A field hospital may lack sufficient resources for provision of anesthesia and thus may not be usable for emergency trauma surgery.
options.C: A pre-made plan to triage patients from overwhelmed hospitals to other trauma centers would be beneficial.
options.D: In a mass-casualty event, additional vascular access and blood products should be requested before losing the tamponade effect after opening the abdomen or chest.

questions.rationale: When fluids and medications are scarce, disaster resources should be allocated after confirming patient need rather than used indiscriminately. Miller supports A.

optionExplanations.A: A directly states Miller’s resource-allocation principle: use scarce disaster medications, fluids, and kits only after confirming patient need.
optionExplanations.B: A field hospital may lack sufficient anesthesia resources, but that limitation does not state how available resources should be allocated.
optionExplanations.C: Preplanned patient redistribution may help overwhelmed hospitals, but it does not provide the bedside allocation rule asked for.
optionExplanations.D: Requesting access and blood before losing tamponade can be important, but that trauma-specific action does not state the general scarcity-allocation principle.

questions.prompt: During organ procurement management, a brain-dead donor develops abrupt high-volume dilute urine output, rising serum sodium, and progressive hypovolemia. Which brain-death-associated disorder best explains this pattern?

options.A: Catecholamine storm from the initial sympathetic discharge.
options.B: Central diabetes insipidus from loss of posterior-pituitary function.
options.C: Vasoplegia from loss of sympathetic tone.
options.D: Hypothermia from loss of hypothalamic thermoregulation.

questions.rationale: After brain death, donors commonly develop major physiologic alterations and hemodynamic instability requiring active management during procurement. Miller supports B.

optionExplanations.A: Goal-directed donor management can increase organs transplanted per donor, but that outcome does not identify the physiologic problem requiring management.
optionExplanations.B: B directly states Miller’s donor problem: brain-death donors often have significant physiologic alterations and hemodynamic instability.
optionExplanations.C: Ischemia-reperfusion injury can impair grafts and may be mitigated, but it is a transplantation complication rather than the donor physiologic problem.
optionExplanations.D: DCD donors experience hypotension before arrest and organ perfusion compromise, but that is a different donation pathway from brain-death donation.

questions.prompt: What can aspiration of a dental appliance cause?

options.A: Aspiration of blood secondary to airway surgery generates marked chest-radiograph changes out of proportion to clinical signs.
options.B: Aspiration of clear oral secretions during induction, mask ventilation, or emergence is common and usually insignificant.
options.C: Aspiration of food, small objects, pieces of teeth, or dental appliances can cause airway obstruction with distal atelectasis or pneumonia.
options.D: Massive blood aspiration or aspiration of clots obstructs airways, interferes with oxygenation, and leads to fibrinous changes in air spaces.

questions.rationale: Aspirated food, teeth, small objects, and dental appliances can obstruct the airway and cause distal atelectasis or pneumonia. Barash supports C.

optionExplanations.A: Blood aspiration after airway surgery can produce radiographic changes, but that does not describe dental-appliance aspiration.
optionExplanations.B: Clear-secretions aspiration is often insignificant, but food or dental-appliance aspiration can produce the obstructive and distal complications asked for.
optionExplanations.C: C directly states Barash’s consequence: aspirated food, teeth, objects, or dental appliances can obstruct the airway and cause distal atelectasis or pneumonia.
optionExplanations.D: Massive blood or clot aspiration can obstruct airways and impair oxygenation, but it is a different aspirate from a dental appliance.

sources: Barash 9e (2023).pdf — 54. Postanesthesia Recovery — PDF p. 4597
questions.evidenceSufficiency: The stored Barash passages directly support C and distinguish blood, secretions, objects, and clot aspiration.

questions.prompt: According to Barash 9th edition, which standard should govern anesthesia and monitoring for an interventional-radiology procedure outside the operating room?
questions.domain: Domain 14 · Interventional radiology and procedural settings

options.A: Allergic reactions to contrast media are a specific hazard in X-ray and interventional-radiology locations.
options.B: Remote anesthesia locations may have restricted access, low light levels, radiation exposure, and unexpected movement of X-ray equipment.
options.C: Nonoperating-room anesthesia equipment must meet the same standards as equipment provided in the operating room, and patients should be transported to an appropriate PACU with anesthesia-trained monitoring.
options.D: Patients must receive the same standard of care at a nonoperating-room site as in the operating room, with applicable anesthesia guidelines.

questions.rationale: Nonoperating-room anesthesia must meet the same standard of care as operating-room anesthesia, with applicable guidelines governing care and monitoring. Barash supports D.

optionExplanations.A: Contrast reactions are a specific interventional-radiology hazard, but they do not state the governing standard of care.
optionExplanations.B: Restricted access, low light, radiation, and moving equipment are remote-location hazards, but hazards do not state the applicable care standard.
optionExplanations.C: Matching equipment standards and PACU monitoring are operational requirements, but the lead-in asks for the overarching anesthesia and monitoring standard.
optionExplanations.D: D directly states Barash’s governing principle: provide the same standard of care outside the operating room, following applicable anesthesia guidelines.

sources: Barash 9e (2023).pdf — 33. Nonoperating Room Anesthesia — PDF p. 2652
Miller 10e (2024).pdf — 68. Ambulatory (Outpatient) Anesthesia — PDF p. 2592
